children: Everyone is qualified. Everyone is compliant. So what could possibly be the problem? The market’s integrity has never felt safer.
A Very Busy Retirement

When MCX inducted Santosh Kumar Mohanty as Public Interest Director on 28 May this year, it did not park him in a corner. He went straight onto the Audit Committee, which oversees financial reporting and statutory compliance. He sits on the exchange's Public Interest Directors' Committee, the PID-only body meant to guard market integrity and investor protection. This apart, he's on the exchange's Risk Management Committee, Standing Committee on Technology, Investment Committee and Member Committee.  All the most sensitive seats in the building, from day one.
Recall what SEBI has had to say to MCX lately.

In May 2025 the regulator fined the exchange Rs 25 lakh for disclosure lapses and inaccurate information on its trading software contract with 63 Moons — payments of Rs 222 crore over three quarters against a previous year's profit of Rs 118 crore, disclosed late.

In this order, SEBI dropped several other allegations while finding only disclosure violations. In 2023, SEBI fined MCX Rs 6 lakh after finding that seven brokers had coded 50 clients as Sikkim residents despite KYC records showing otherwise. One client accounted for 95% of Sikkim-linked trading. SEBI found MCX had failed to detect it. Then came the trading halts, the financial disincentives for technical glitches, the four-hour outage last October that pushed trading to the disaster recovery site.
Disclosure adequacy. Committee procedure. Compliance. Exactly the subject matter of the committees Mr Mohanty now sits on.

His qualification is unmatched, because until June 2023 he sat on the other side. He came to SEBI from the Forward Markets Commission in 2015 to run the commodity derivatives department built after the merger, then served five years as Whole Time Member holding market regulation, commodity derivatives and international affairs. He knows the file, the format, the officers and what happens inside SEBI when a reply is found wanting. Boards do not pay for a nameplate.
Now the part nobody at either institution wants spelled out.

He has not actually left SEBI's side of the table. SEBI's own website lists the High Powered Advisory Committee on settlement orders and compounding of offences: Justice (Retd.) Jai Narayan Patel as chairman, with N. Venkatram, S.K. Mohanty and Sarit Jafa. This is the committee that examines what an alleged wrongdoer has offered and sends its recommendation to SEBI's Whole Time Members. The final authority lies with SEBI's decision-making structure, including the Panel of Whole Time Members in the relevant process. But the recommendation carries its weight.
So consider the position.

A member of the committee that examines and recommends settlement terms to SEBI's decision-makers, and simultaneously sits on the audit and nomination committees of an exchange SEBI supervises. He also serves on the boards of entities operating in areas regulated by SEBI, including Acuite Ratings & Research, Computer Age Management Services, Bajaj Finserv Asset Management and SBI CDMDF Trustee. That does not establish a conflict in any particular matter. It does, however, create a question of institutional overlap: the same former SEBI WTM is advising the regulator on settlement matters while serving in governance roles at entities within the regulator's wider supervisory perimeter.
The conflict is not hypothetical in its consequences. It is structural, and it runs in three directions.

Downward. An exchange is a first-level regulator of its own members. Through the PID committee, a man who advises SEBI on settlements helps also decide regulatory action against brokers — some of whom may later seek settlements from SEBI. MCX is a market infrastructure institution whose regulatory functions include oversight of its members. Mohanty now serves on its Public Interest Directors' Committee while separately serving on SEBI's settlement advisory committee.

Upward. MCX's executive appointments require SEBI's approval; the exchange announced clearances for executive directors on 27 May, the same day SEBI cleared him. He sits on the committee that selects those executives and on a committee that advises the regulator which must approve them. SEBI's approval for Mohanty's appointment was dated May 27; MCX's announcement records his appointment from May 28. The exchange also announced SEBI approvals for executive-director appointments on May 27.

Sideways. When any of these entities does have a matter before the HPAC, he must recuse. SEBI's settlement rules require a quorum of three, as the regulator discovered in 2017 when two members recused in the NSE co-location consent case and the panel had to be reworked. A member with five regulated hats may be a recusal problem waiting to be scheduled? The regulations already contemplate recusal. The question is how frequently such recusals could arise when a member of the settlement committee also holds multiple positions within entities that fall within SEBI's regulatory perimeter.
The rules currently do not appear to impose a blanket prohibition on this combination of roles.

The 1992 service rules bar a retired Whole Time Member from taking employment for one year, waivable with the Centre's sanction. The new code adopted in June 2026 bars former WTMs for two years from appearing before or against SEBI — the provision addresses appearances before or against SEBI; it does not, on its face, create a general two-year prohibition on board appointments at entities within SEBI's regulatory perimeter. Parliament's Standing Committee on Finance has asked for the one year to be made two.

Mohanty is also in good company. G Mahalingam returned after retirement to chair SEBI's Secondary Market Advisory Committee. M S Sahoo, the former SEBI whole time member, returned to Chair its Market Data Advisory Committee in 2022. S Ravindran got the Intermediary Advisory Committee, which advises on exchanges, while sitting on NSE's board. Ananta Barua left in 2023 for a law firm advisory role and IFSCA's fund management committee.

The regulator regulates a market whose boardrooms it has furnished itself. Everyone is qualified. Everyone is compliant. And when the next show-cause notice reaches Exchange Square, everyone involved will already be on first-name terms.

The issue is not whether these former regulators are qualified. They may plainly be. Nor is the issue whether a former SEBI official should ever serve on a regulated entity's board. The rules permit substantial movement between public regulatory expertise and private-sector governance. The harder question is whether the safeguards are sufficient when the same former regulator sits on both sides of the regulatory perimeter — advising SEBI on settlement matters while serving in governance roles at entities that operate within its regulatory universe.
There may be no rule prohibiting the arrangement. But that is precisely why the question deserves to be asked in public.
Palak Shah

BW Reporters Palak Shah is a seasoned investigative journalist and the fearless author of The Market Mafia: Chronicle of India’s High-Tech Stock Market Scandal & The Cabal That Went Scot-Free, a hard-hitting exposé that unmasked the shadowy underbelly of India’s financial markets. With nearly two decades of boots-on-the-ground reporting in Mumbai, Palak has carved a reputation as a relentless truth-seeker, diving deep into the nexus of money, power, and regulation.

His bylines have graced India’s most prestigious financial dailies, including The Economic Times, Business Standard, The Financial Express, and The Hindu Business Line, where his incisive coverage has shaped narratives and rattled boardrooms. Drawn to crime reporting at the tender age of 19, Palak quickly realized that Mumbai’s gritty gang wars of the 1980s had given way to a slicker, more insidious form of organized crime—white-collar schemes orchestrated in corporate towers.

This epiphany fueled his pivot to financial journalism, where he’s spent years decoding the complex machinations of India’s ‘white money’ economy. From stock market manipulations to regulatory loopholes, Palak’s work peels back the polished veneer of high finance to reveal the cabals pulling the strings. His passion for uncovering truth, backed by a knack for connecting dots others miss, makes him a formidable voice in Indian journalism, unafraid to challenge the status quo and expose the players who think they’re untouchable.
